item.title: How Much Change Can an Organisation Actually Absorb?
item.description:
There is a lot of excitement around AI-enabled modernisation, and with good reason. Analysis can be accelerated, code can be generated or transformed faster, testing can be improved, and large estates that once looked prohibitively expensive to tackle can begin to look much more manageable. But that creates a new problem: if the technology can move faster, how much change can the organisation actually absorb?

That question is rarely asked clearly enough at the beginning of a modernisation programme. We tend to model engineering capacity, delivery waves, migration throughput, environments and technical dependencies in some detail, but we do not always model with the same discipline the capacity of the organisation itself to consume the change being produced. That matters because transformation is not complete when the new capability exists. It is complete when the organisation has actually moved.

item.title: Scaling AI Modernisation Means Scaling Decisions, Not Just Code
item.description:
There is a growing assumption in software modernisation that AI will allow us to industrialise the analysis and transformation of existing estates. Give a model a codebase, define the target architecture and increasingly it can analyse, refactor, generate tests and produce a substantial amount of the target implementation.

There is clearly value in that, but the idea becomes much harder when we move from an individual application to an enterprise estate. The problem is not simply that organisations use different technologies. There can be enormous variation between two applications built in the same language, by the same organisation and notionally against the same standards. Years of design decisions, local conventions, framework choices, technical debt, developer preferences and changing architectural standards leave each application carrying part of its own history.

item.title: The Real Power of Agentic Systems Is Closing the Loop
item.description: There is a lot being written about AI agents at the moment, and much of the conversation understandably focuses on autonomy: agents that can execute tasks, call tools, communicate with other systems and increasingly operate across whole workflows. I think that risks missing one of the more interesting opportunities, because the real power of agentic systems is not simply that they can act. It is that they can close the loop between information, ownership, decisions and change.

item.title: Borrowing Horizons
item.description:
My seven-year-old daughter spends quite a lot of time thinking about the future, usually in the form of questions for me.

“When can I ride a motorbike?” “When can I use that power tool?” “When can I jump off that?”

Sometimes she wants a date. Is it when she’s eight? Ten? A teenager? Sometimes tomorrow seems perfectly reasonable.

What I find fascinating is the ambition behind the questions. She can imagine herself doing almost anything; what she doesn’t yet have is a particularly sophisticated understanding of the risks, dependencies or capabilities involved in getting there. Her horizon is enormous because experience hasn’t yet taught her all the reasons something might be difficult.

item.title: From Coding Agents to Loop Engineering: Building Engineering Memory for AI
item.description: Most AI coding setups still look suspiciously like a faster version of the way we have always developed software. A developer asks for a change, an AI model explores some files, writes some code, perhaps runs a few tests, and returns the result. Add more specialised agents and the flow becomes more sophisticated — an architect creates a plan, an explorer inspects the repository, a developer implements the change and a reviewer checks the result — but fundamentally it is still a pipeline.

item.title: When Trust Becomes the Constraint
item.description:
One of the more difficult problems I keep coming back to with AI-assisted software modernisation isn’t really a technology problem. It’s trust.

We have all seen an LLM confidently make something up, merge two facts that happened to look similar, or produce an explanation that sounds entirely reasonable until someone who really understands the domain reads it. Once you have seen that happen a few times, it changes how you approach the capability, and that matters when we start asking AI to help modernise software.

item.title: Lowering the Cost of Curiosity
item.description:
I have been doing a lot of experimentation with local models recently, as have many of my colleagues. There is also a growing anticipation around the next generation of developer workstations and AI-focused boxes: machines capable of running increasingly useful models without sending every request to a SaaS platform.

It is easy to see this as another technology choice: local versus cloud, open model versus proprietary model, workstation versus API. I think the more interesting question for enterprises is economic.
